Drzewica Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Drzewica, Poland

Demolished. Jews are first recorded in Drzewica in the 18th century, with a kehilla by 1765; population reached 61% (1,013) by 1921, mostly murdered at Treblinka in 1942. This cemetery formally resulted from an October 14, 1865 government decision establishing a separate Synagogue District in Drzewica. Poland's local council voted to close the cemetery on September 24, 1962, followed by a May 14, 1964 liquidation resolution; the Minister of Municipal Economy signed the formal closure order June 22, 1964, permitting alternate uses four days later, with documentation noting the last burial in 1943. A 1965 provincial proposal suggested either tree planting or expanding a nearby industrial plant onto the site. A 1985 official cemetery survey bluntly noted 'there are no elements characteristic of a Jewish cemetery,' describing sand-extraction pits, an illegal dump, and numerous human bones, concluding the site 'does not function as a cemetery in the public awareness.'
